newsitem.title: CHINA: S.Korea yet to find solution on N.Korean defector.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea yet to find solution on N.Korean defector.

text.p: South Korean officials said on Monday a senior Pyongyang defector holed up in Seoul's mission in Beijing could leave as soon as this week but a dispute with China over his destination was stalling a solution on his fate.
Hwang Jang-yop, North Korea's top ideologue and senior aide to supreme leader Kim Jong-il, has languished in South Korea's consular compound in Beijing since he sought asylum there on February 12.
"It could be this week, it could be next week," South Korean embassy spokesman Chang Moon-Ik said when asked when Hwang would leave Beijing.

Officials in Seoul said Hwang, the most senior official to flee his beleaguered Stalinist homeland, would fly to a third country this week after China and South Korea hammer out fine details of his departure.
A dispute with Beijing over where Hwang would be taken was the main point holding up resolution of his fate, Chang said by telephone.
"In principle we want to bring him to Korea but... we may have to find another way," he said.

China's Foreign Ministry refused to comment on Hwang's fate, saying they could report no new developments since Premier Li Peng said last Friday that conditions were nearly ripe for a solution to the diplomatic crisis.
The defection of Hwang, the most senior official to abandon his Stalinist homeland, has muddied ties between China and the two Koreas, bitter rivals since the 1950-1953 Korean War.
Beijing must decide whether to hand over Hwang to new business partner Seoul while giving full consideration to the concerns of old communist ally Pyongyang.

Security around Seoul's consulate was tight on Monday. Chinese police armed with assault rifles were posted at approaches to the compound, backed by several armoured personnel carriers and a crowd control truck.
In Seoul, another South Korean foreign ministry official said Beijing and Seoul had agreed that Hwang would be sent to a third country before being allowed asylum in South Korea.
"Hwang Jang-yop will be able to leave China this week but his departure might not be today or tomorrow," a senior Seoul foreign ministry official told reporters.
"He will have to stay in a third country for a considerable period of time before coming to South Korea," said the official, who declined to be identified.
He said the Philippines was one of several "transit points" being considered.
Three vans seen driving away from Seoul's consulate in the Chinese capital early on Monday had fuelled speculation Hwang had been spirited out of the heavily-guarded compound.
Philippine Foreign Secretary Domingo Siazon, visiting Tokyo, said he did not know if Hwang had already been moved to his country.
Siazon said on Saturday his country had been asked to serve as a transit point for Hwang if he were allowed to leave for South Korea.
A top Manila Foreign Office official said Hwang would likely stay in the Philippines for a few days, but added that it was possible his country was being used as a decoy.
